spans.t: This is a small book for eight slow days. It is made to go with the Camino Aragonés, the road that runs from Somport, in the Pyrenees, to Puente la Reina, ~160 km. The app's own notes on this route describe a mountain start and then rolling hills, a quiet road, and services that are sparse in places.

You read one day at a time, whether you are walking or at home. At home, the morning part wants five quiet minutes and the evening part the last three before the light goes out. If your road takes more days than the book, repeat a favourite or rest. If it takes fewer, read the day that fits the day you are having.
The songs

The book is built on fifteen psalms, Psalms 120 to 134. Their headings call them songs of ascents, and they are traditionally understood as the songs pilgrims sang as they went up to Jerusalem, a city on high ground; the Bible speaks of travelling to it as going up. Scholars differ on how they were really used, and the next chapter says what is known and what is not. What is plain is what is in them: a road, hills, a gate, danger, tears, tiredness, waiting for morning, and a house at the end. That is why they travel well.
The psalms keep their own order, two by two, with the last one on its own on the eighth day. The order happens to be a road.

items.t: Days 1 and 2 (Psalms 120 to 123).
Distress and setting out, then gladness at the city, and contempt.
Days 3 and 4 (Psalms 124 to 127).
Help in danger, then a return, tears and the work of building.
Days 5 and 6 (Psalms 128 to 131).
A household and a long affliction, then out of the depths and a quiet heart.
Days 7 and 8 (Psalms 132 to 134).
A house for God, people living together in unity, and a blessing at night.

spans.t: A day, in two parts
In the morning
there are three parts.

items.t: The passage.

Two short stretches of psalm, in the exact words of the World English Bible, one for each psalm of the day. Read each one twice, and say the second reading aloud, or nearly aloud. These were songs before they were pages. Where verses are left out, a mark like this shows it: …, and the reflection tells you what is missing.
The reflection.
This part is ours. It starts from something on the road and lets the psalms open it. It says what they say, where they are hard, and what they might ask of an ordinary day. It is allowed to doubt.
For the walk.
A question to carry for an hour and one small practice that needs nothing but attention.

spans.t: In the evening
there are two more.

items.t: At the end of the day.
A look back at the day you have lived, with the psalms in mind, and two or three gentle questions. Nothing needs writing down.
A short prayer.
Plain words of our own, not the psalmists'. Say it as a prayer if you pray. Change a word where your own tradition would. If you do not pray, take it as a wish.

spans.t: Hebrew poems, shared

The psalms are Hebrew poems. They were Jewish before they were Christian, and both traditions have prayed them for a very long time. They are addressed to God and speak as believers, and we say so plainly so that nobody is surprised. People walk for many reasons: faith, sport, grief, curiosity, a rest from work. All are welcome here. You do not have to share the psalmists' faith to know what they are describing. You will meet the name Yahweh in the first line; the next chapter explains it.

Some of the fifteen are hard. A few ask for harm to fall on enemies, and one makes a household into a picture that many lives do not fit. The reflections say so when it happens and do not tidy it away.
Before you set out

A psalm is not a weather forecast. In the mountains, check the forecast the evening before, start early, carry water and food, and tell someone your plan. Services can be few, so know where your next water is. For anything that worries you, see a doctor. In an emergency in Spain or France, call 112.
Two words you will meet.
Albergue
means a pilgrim hostel: a simple place to sleep, usually in bunks, sometimes with a kitchen you share with strangers.
Buen Camino
is the greeting walkers give one another on the way, a wish that the road goes well.
Read slowly. A short song can carry a long day.
The Psalms
The Book of Psalms is a collection of 150 poems, songs and prayers in the Hebrew Bible, which Christians call the Old Testament. Its Hebrew name,
Tehillim

, means "praises", though many of the poems are complaints, and many are both. The collection falls into five books, and the songs of this book are in the last of them, which runs from Psalm 107 to Psalm 150.

Tradition gave many psalms to David, the king. Others carry the names of different singers, and many carry no name at all. Scholars differ on how old the poems are and how the collection grew. Many think the collection took its final shape in the centuries after the return from exile in Babylon (about the sixth century BC), with some poems older than that. This book claims nothing more precise.
The Songs of Ascents
Fifteen psalms, 120 to 134, carry the same heading. In Hebrew it is
shir ha-ma'alot

, which is usually put into English as a song of ascents, or of steps, or of going up. Four of the fifteen are headed with David's name (122, 124, 131 and 133) and one with Solomon's (127). The other ten name nobody. Whether the headings are the poets' own or were added later, scholars weigh differently.

What the heading means, and how the songs were used, are also open questions. The most familiar answer, and the one this book takes as a starting point, is that they are traditionally understood as songs pilgrims sang while going up to Jerusalem for the great festivals. There are others. An early Jewish tradition, written down in the Mishnah (about AD 200), speaks of fifteen steps in the Temple, one for each song, on which the Levites sang. Some link the word to the going up from exile. Some point to the poems' own habit of climbing by repetition, one line picking up a word from the one before (Psalm 121, with its "keeps" and "keeper", is a good example). No one can settle it, and the book does not need to. What matters for a walker is simpler. These are short poems, all but one of them nine verses long or shorter, with a road and its weather in them: hills, a gate, a stream in dry country, a watchman waiting for morning. They are easy to carry, and they are honest about fear and tiredness.
A practical point. Some Bibles, following the old Greek and Latin numbering, call these Psalms 119 to 133. If your Bible disagrees with the numbers here by one, that is why.
Jewish and Christian use

The psalms are Jewish poems, and Jews have sung and prayed them in synagogue and at home from ancient times. Psalm 126, for example, is sung in many communities before the blessing after meals on Sabbaths and festivals. Christians have prayed the psalms from the earliest centuries, and Latin-speaking Christians called these fifteen the gradual psalms, from the Latin for a step. They are shared ground, and this book tries to respect both houses. Where a reading belongs to one tradition (in Psalm 132, for example), the reflection says whose it is.
The psalms use
Israel
for the people who sang them, and
Zion
for the hill of Jerusalem and then for the city and its people. We read them as ancient poems and say nothing about any present-day politics.
The name Yahweh
You will meet the word
Yahweh

in the first line. It is how the World English Bible prints the personal name of God in Hebrew, written with four consonants. Most English Bibles print "the LORD" in capital letters instead. In Jewish tradition the name is held so holy that many do not say it aloud and say
Adonai
, "my Lord", or
HaShem
, "the Name", in its place. The World English Bible also uses
Yah
, a short form of the name, and keeps the word
Lord
for
Adonai

We quote the translation as it stands, and we handle the name with care. If you are used to saying "the Lord", say that. If the name is not one you say, say the word you do say. The sense of the poems will not suffer.
The translation, the edition and the licence

The passages are from the World English Bible, a modern English translation made by volunteers. It is based on the American Standard Version of 1901, brought up to date, and it has been dedicated to the public domain. We read it from the complete text on Project Gutenberg, ebook number 8294, and every quotation in this book was checked against that text, word for word.

The passages are untouched, apart from the verse numbers and headings, which are left out. The translators' punctuation is kept, straight quotation marks and all. Where we skip verses inside a psalm, a mark like this shows it: …. Nine of the fifteen psalms are quoted whole. Six are quoted in part, and each reflection says what was left out. The choice of passages, their order, the reflections, the questions and the prayers are ours and are original. The prayers are written plainly, in our own words, and do not pretend to be Scripture.
No Project Gutenberg licence text or trademark is copied into this book.
Where does my help come from?
The passage

paras.t: In my distress, I cried to Yahweh. He answered me. Deliver my soul, Yahweh, from lying lips, from a deceitful tongue. … Woe is me, that I live in Meshech, that I dwell among the tents of Kedar! My soul has had her dwelling too long with him who hates peace. I am for peace, but when I speak, they are for war.

cite.t: — Psalm 120:1 to 2 and 5 to 7 (World English Bible)

paras.t: I will lift up my eyes to the hills. Where does my help come from? My help comes from Yahweh, who made heaven and earth. He will not allow your foot to be moved. He who keeps you will not slumber. Behold, he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep. Yahweh is your keeper. Yahweh is your shade on your right hand. The sun will not harm you by day, nor the moon by night. Yahweh will keep you from all evil. He will keep your soul. Yahweh will keep your going out and your coming in, from this time forth, and forevermore.

spans.t: Reflection

At the foot of a long climb there is a moment when you add everything up. The slope, the hours, the weight on your back, the water left in the bottle. On the Camino Aragonés the moment may come early, since the road starts in the Pyrenees and the app's notes call it a mountain start. Whatever your road is, you know the look that goes up to the ridge and asks a question.
Psalm 121 opens with that look:
I will lift up my eyes to the hills.

Readers have taken the line in two ways. In one, the hills are the danger, with their high places, their weather and whoever might be waiting there, and the question is a worried one. In the other, the hills are where hope points, towards Jerusalem and the house of God. Scholars differ, and the Hebrew will carry either. The answer carries both: help comes from the one
who made heaven and earth
. It does not come from the hills themselves, and it is not stopped by them.
But the day begins one poem earlier, with someone a long way from home.
In my distress, I cried to Yahweh. He answered me.

Notice the order. The first of the fifteen songs has a cry and an answer in its first breath, before anything else has happened. Then the complaint comes, and it is a very human one. The poet is surrounded by lying lips and by people who want a fight:
I am for peace, but when I speak, they are for war.

Anyone who has sat at a table where everyone was angry knows that loneliness. Meshech and Kedar are the names of distant peoples, one far to the north of Israel and the other out among the desert tents. The poet is probably not living in either. Many scholars read the names as a figure of speech for being so far from home that any place might as well be those.

Many people set out on a long walk to get away from something: a job, a house, an argument, a loss. The first two songs hold both halves of that. One is the leaving, with its tiredness of other people's noise. The other is the standing at the bottom of the hill, looking up. You may be in either today, or in both before lunch.
The passage is hard in two places. The first is in Psalm 120, between the stretches we have quoted. Verses 3 and 4 turn on the liar, and the answer is a line of its own:
Sharp arrows of the mighty, with coals of juniper.

The poet, hurt by lies, sees harm coming to the liar, and perhaps wants it. It is the first of several such verses in these fifteen songs, and we leave them off the page, not out of the book. Wanting someone who deceived you to pay is an old and honest feeling, and the psalm is honest enough to put it down. You do not have to make it a plan.

The second is the promise at the end of Psalm 121: the sun will not harm you, and you will be kept from all evil. Read flatly, as an insurance policy, that is not true to the world. Walkers get burnt and dehydrated, they fall, and some are hurt on roads that could not be called dangerous. Anyone who has lost someone on a road will not be comforted by a sentence that says it cannot happen. One way to read it is as trust rather than as a guarantee: a walker who is not alone, kept in a deeper sense than being spared. Others find even that too much, and that is allowed. The psalm does not cancel the forecast. Carry water, check the weather the night before, and start early. Day 3 says more about danger.

What does it ask of an ordinary day? Only to lift the eyes. Not away from the path, but beyond your own feet, to see where you are. And there is a last line to take with you, the sense of the whole walk in a few words:
your going out and your coming in
. You go out of the door in the morning and you come in at night, and the psalm claims both ends of the day.
For the walk

items.t: What do I look at first when I am afraid or tired, my feet or the horizon? What would it be to look at the other one for a minute?

At the next rise, stop and take three breaths. Lift your eyes to the farthest thing you can see and name it quietly: a ridge, a tower, a line of trees, the sky. Then look down at the path and go on. Do it once or twice today, not more. If the day is flat and nothing rises, do it at the next bench or gate.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Boots off. The first evening of a walk is mostly arithmetic: how far, how long, how much is left, and what the feet think of it. They will tell you plainly. Let them have their say, and then think about the other things the day contained.

You lifted your eyes today, or you did not. If you did, what was there? A ridge in the morning haze, a village that looked closer than it was, a bird, a very ordinary cloud. If you kept your head down against the slope, that is not a failure. Head-down is how most hills are climbed. But there may have been one moment when the road opened out and you could have looked up. It may come tomorrow.

Think too about what you left behind in order to be here. Perhaps it was only a sink of dishes and a phone that kept pinging. Perhaps it was larger. Psalm 120 does not hurry the poet past the distress. It lets it be said, once, in the first line, and it is answered. You might let it be said tonight: whatever you are carrying in from the other life, say what it is, plainly, even if only to the ceiling.

Then look for the answers, the small ones, because the poem is as interested in the answer as in the cry, and tired people forget to count them. A bench at the right moment. A nod from a stranger. A cloud across the sun at noon. A tap that ran cold when you needed it. No need to give any of it a name. Count it, that is all.
And there is the plain fact of the evening. This morning you went out, and tonight you have come in. The psalm claims both ends of the day, and so can you, if only because it is done.

Be honest about the tiredness. The first day is rarely the real one. Your body has not decided yet whether to be an ally, and your mind has not yet quietened. A bed that is not your own, a snore across the room, a light that clicks on at five. None of that is a sign that the walk is a mistake. It is a sign that it has begun, and that it will take some days to find its pace.

One practical kindness for the person who wakes tomorrow: fill the bottle, put the socks where you will find them, look at the forecast. The psalm's keeping is on a large scale, but a keeper's work is mostly small preparations like these, and you can do a little of it for yourself.

items.t: Where did I lift my eyes today, and what did I see when I did?
What am I glad to have left behind, and what am I carrying anyway?
When I say I am being kept, what do I really rely on: the plan, the forecast, my own stubbornness, something else?

spans.t: A short prayer

Tonight I put the pack down. Thank you for the road that held me today. Whatever I left behind, let it weigh a little less by morning. Keep my feet sound and my temper kind. If I do not know who is listening, let this be a wish.
Can gladness at the gate and a sneer from the comfortable sit in the same day?
The passage

paras.t: I was glad when they said to me, "Let's go to Yahweh's house!" Our feet are standing within your gates, Jerusalem; Jerusalem, that is built as a city that is compact together; where the tribes go up, even Yah's tribes, according to an ordinance for Israel, to give thanks to the name of Yahweh. … Pray for the peace of Jerusalem. Those who love you will prosper. Peace be within your walls, and prosperity within your palaces. For my brothers' and companions' sakes, I will now say, "Peace be within you." For the sake of the house of Yahweh our God, I will seek your good.

cite.t: — Psalm 122:1 to 4 and 6 to 9 (World English Bible)

paras.t: To you I do lift up my eyes, you who sit in the heavens. Behold, as the eyes of servants look to the hand of their master, as the eyes of a maid to the hand of her mistress; so our eyes look to Yahweh, our God, until he has mercy on us. Have mercy on us, Yahweh, have mercy on us, for we have endured much contempt. Our soul is exceedingly filled with the scoffing of those who are at ease, with the contempt of the proud.

spans.t: Reflection

Some mornings you are glad before you are properly awake. Someone nearby is lacing their boots and says, "Shall we go?", and the answer rises from somewhere that has nothing to do with sleep. Psalm 122 begins there.
I was glad when they said to me
, the poet says, and what they said was an invitation. The gladness does not start with the poet. It arrives from outside, from being asked, from the fact that other people are going too.
Notice who goes:
where the tribes go up

. It is a crowd, a whole people on the move, climbing together to give thanks. A road can be lonely, and some days you will want it to be. But on a long walk company also comes and goes, for an hour, for a day, for a table in the evening, and the psalm treats company as part of the gladness and not an extra.
Then the poem does what pilgrim poems do. It arrives.
Our feet are standing within your gates, Jerusalem.

The tense changes in the middle of the song. For days the city has been a word on a sign or a distance in a book, and now the feet are on its stones. If you have ever come over a rise and seen the place you have been walking towards, you know the odd quiet that follows. The psalm stays there a moment and looks at the city,
built as a city that is compact together
, close-packed and held tight.
What the traveller does with the arrival is the surprise. Having come, the poet does not boast of it. The poet prays for the place:
Pray for the peace of Jerusalem.
And the reason is given, and it is warm:
For my brothers' and companions' sakes, I will now say
, and what is said is
Peace be within you.
A guest blesses the host's town. It is a good habit for anyone passing through. A village is somebody's home and not a backdrop, and a
buenos días
to someone at a door is a small form of the same prayer.

One verse is missing from the page, and it matters. Verse 5 says that there are thrones set there for judgment, the thrones of David's house. The city is a capital with a king's court, and this is a political poem as well as a pilgrim's one. Its peace is a peace of justice and order, and of one family's rule. You can hold the prayer for peace and leave the thrones, and many readers do.
Psalm 123 does not let the gladness last the page. It takes up the lifted eyes of the first day,
To you I do lift up my eyes

, but the mood has changed. The picture is of servants watching a master's hand, and it will sit badly with some readers. It comes from a world of household service and bondage, and we do not take it as approval of that world. What it describes is a kind of attention: not watching a master's face to flatter, but watching the hand, for the smallest sign that mercy is coming. If the picture grates, set another beside it, such as a child watching a door or a walker watching a gap in the cloud. The poem asks only for the eyes, fixed on one place and waiting.
And the reason for the waiting is plain:
we have endured much contempt
, and
the scoffing of those who are at ease

. The singers have been looked down on by people comfortable enough to find them funny. You may meet a thin version on any road, a remark about why anyone would walk when there are buses, or an older sneer you have carried since you were small, and that the road has a way of waking. The psalm does not answer the sneer, and it does not fight it. It looks up, and it waits for mercy.
Gladness at the gate is real, and so is contempt, and the psalms put them side by side without apology.

Three small things, then. Be glad when someone says "Let's go", and let it be a plain gladness. Wish peace on the place you pass through, whether or not it knows. And when a sneer finds you, do not stare at it. Lift the eyes to where mercy comes from.
For the walk

items.t: Who has made this day possible, a host, a friend at home, someone who simply set out at the same time? Have I thanked them, even silently?
As you come to the next village, hamlet or farm, wish it peace in your own words before you go in. Then greet the first person you see, in their language if you can. A plain
buenos días
is enough.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Gladness is easier to find at seven in the morning than at seven in the evening, so look for it now with a kinder eye. It need not have been large. A coffee that came at the right moment, a downhill after a long up, a stranger who laughed at the same thing you did. Count whatever there was.

The psalm's gladness came from being asked in. Was there an asking today? A good morning offered first, a door held, a seat made room for, a loaf passed along a table. These are easy to miss when you are watching your feet, and they are the whole of what a road gives you apart from the road.
And look at where you arrived. The psalm's feet were
standing within your gates

. Yours are standing inside today's gate, wherever it was: a village square, a hostel door, a bench at the end of the stage. Notice them. They did the whole thing. Take your boots off and thank the feet, aloud if the room allows.
The poet's reason for blessing the city was other people:
my brothers' and companions' sakes

, the song says, so the arrival was for them too. Who were your companions today? Some walked beside you and some only passed. Some are at home and walked in your thoughts. Wish them peace by name, one at a time. It takes about a minute.

Then think about the places you passed through. Some of them you will have walked straight past as though they were scenery. It is not too late. Pick one, a street or a square or a lane with a washing line across it, and wish it peace now, in your own words. It costs nothing, and it is a kind way to leave a place.

Notice, too, where you waited today with your eyes on somebody's hand: the person with the key, the driver at the crossing, whoever was deciding whether the kitchen was open. Waiting for a small mercy is a daily posture on a road, and you may have taken it up without knowing.

And did anyone look down on you today? It may have been a passing car, a remark, a glance at your boots, or a memory that came up on the hill without being asked. Notice where your eyes went when it stung. Did they stay on the sting, or did they lift? Forgiving it is not tonight's job. You only have to notice, and set it down for the night.

Tiredness makes the stings sharper. A remark lands harder at five in the afternoon than at nine in the morning, and a small insult can seem a large one when the body is empty. Eat something, drink water, wash, and judge the day afterwards, not before.

items.t: Where today was I glad, and who or what had asked me into it?
Which place or person did I pass that I could wish peace on tonight?
When something stung, where did I turn my eyes?

spans.t: A short prayer

For the gladness that found me today, thank you. For the places I passed through and the people who live in them, peace. For the sting I carried, let it lose its hold before morning. Let me sleep like someone who is expected somewhere tomorrow.
What do you say after a narrow escape?
The passage

paras.t: If it had not been Yahweh who was on our side, let Israel now say, if it had not been Yahweh who was on our side, when men rose up against us; then they would have swallowed us up alive, when their wrath was kindled against us; then the waters would have overwhelmed us, the stream would have gone over our soul; then the proud waters would have gone over our soul. Blessed be Yahweh, who has not given us as a prey to their teeth. Our soul has escaped like a bird out of the fowler's snare. The snare is broken, and we have escaped. Our help is in the name of Yahweh, who made heaven and earth.
Those who trust in Yahweh are as Mount Zion, which can't be moved, but remains forever. As the mountains surround Jerusalem, so Yahweh surrounds his people from this time forth and forevermore.

spans.t: Reflection

Sooner or later a walk has a narrow place in it. A stretch of road with a car coming too fast and no verge. A wet stone that turns under the foot. A sky that darkens faster than the forecast said it would, or a stream higher than you expected. Nothing happens, you get through, and ten minutes later your hands are still a little shaky. What do you say, after that?
Psalm 124 is a song for the other side of a narrow place. Its first words are in the past tense:
If it had not been Yahweh who was on our side.
That "if" is the grammar of people who got through. And look how it insists. The poet says it once, then says to the whole people,
let Israel now say
, and then says it again. Gratitude here is not only felt. It is said, aloud, together, and the saying is part of how the rescue is remembered.

The dangers come in four pictures, and each is a way that fear feels. Being swallowed alive. Being drowned by water that goes over the head. Being torn by teeth. Being trapped. Then the last picture is the lightest of all:
Our soul has escaped like a bird out of the fowler's snare.
And notice how the sentence is built. The bird does not break the snare.
The snare is broken
, and the bird is simply out. All the credit goes away from the one who escaped. The song closes on a line you will meet again before the book is over:
Our help is in the name of Yahweh, who made heaven and earth.

What might that ask of an ordinary day? A small act. When you have got through a narrow place, stop, even for ten seconds, and say thank you out loud. Who it is addressed to can stay vague. The saying matters more than the grammar.

There are two hard places today. The first is the very form of the poem. "If it had not been" is the language of survivors. It cannot be said by those who were not rescued, or about them, and the psalm does not say what to say to the ones the flood took. We will not pretend that it does. If you are walking because someone did not come through something, today may be a hard day. It is fine to read only the second psalm, or to put the page down.

The second is in Psalm 125, in the verses left out of the passage. Verses 3 to 5 sort the world into the upright and the crooked, and promise that the crooked will be led away with those who do wrong. Real lives are not so tidy, and the line between the two runs through every person, you included. Read it, if you read it, as a hope that the rule of cruelty will not last for ever, and keep it away from the person snoring in the next bunk.
What stays on the page is better. After the water, the mountains.
As the mountains surround Jerusalem, so Yahweh surrounds his people.

On the first day the hills were a question, threat or hope. Here they have an answer. The poet looks round at the hills that ring the city and sees no trap, only a wall that guards. And the ones who trust are like a mountain that
can't be moved
. That does not mean never shaken. It means staying where you are, with weight in the right place.

A mountain that surrounds you can also hide the weather, and a psalm is not a forecast. This is the calm part, so read it plainly. Before a high or long day, look at the forecast the evening before. Start early, so that you are down from the high ground before the afternoon. Carry water and food and a warm layer you hope not to need. Tell someone where you are going. Turn back if the day looks wrong: there is no shame in turning back. The app's notes say that services are sparse in places on this road, so know where your next water and food are. If you are in trouble, call 112, which works across Spain and France. Trust and a forecast do not compete. Do both.
For the walk

items.t: What is one narrow place I have come through, on this road or in my life, that I have never thanked anyone for?

Before the hardest or highest stretch of the day, stop and check three things: water, weather, and who knows where you are. Go on. When it is behind you, stop again and say "thank you" aloud, to whoever or whatever you like, even to the path itself. If the day brings no narrow place at all, say it for the ones that did not come.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Think of the narrowest place you passed today. It may not have been dramatic. A narrow bridge, a road with no shoulder, a descent on loose stones, an awkward conversation. Whatever it was, you came through it, or you would not be sitting here.

The psalm teaches a habit: go back over the day and say "if it had not been". If it had not been for the foot that held, the driver who moved over, the water bottle that was full, the text that arrived in time, the stranger who pointed out the turn. Most of the things that could have gone wrong did not, and they passed so quietly that you did not notice. Say them now, one by one, and let each be a small thank you.

But some things did go wrong. A blister, a wrong turn, a wasted hour, a sharp word. The psalm has nothing to say about those, and it is an honest silence. Not every day is a rescue. Some days are only a wound, and you tend it. A day of small harms is not a day without help. It may only be a day when the help was less dramatic.

Tiredness plays tricks about danger. When you are tired you can magnify a small risk into a threat, or ignore a real one because you are too weary to care. Neither is fair to you. Check the plain facts instead. What does tomorrow's forecast say? Where is the next water? Does anyone know where you will be? These are small acts of care, and they sit comfortably beside the psalm.
The psalm asks for the thanks to be said,
let Israel now say

, and not only felt. So say one thank-you aloud before you sleep, quietly if the room is asleep: to the ceiling, to the day, to whoever you have in mind. It may feel foolish for a moment. It does not feel foolish for long.

Is there a snare you are still in? A loop of worry that went round all afternoon, or a remark you keep replaying. The psalm's bird did not break the snare itself, and you cannot break yours by thinking harder. Put the loop down for the night and go to sleep without solving it. Things usually look looser in the morning.

And think of being surrounded. Tonight you are among other sleepers, in a village you do not know, with walls around you and hills beyond the walls. You are, quite simply, held by a good deal that you did not arrange.

items.t: What went right today that could easily have gone otherwise, and have I said so to anyone?
Where did I feel hemmed in today, and what, looked at again, was on my side?
What do I need to know about tomorrow before I sleep?

spans.t: A short prayer

Thank you for the foot that held and the car that moved over. Thank you for the water when I needed it. For those who did not come through, I have no words, only this quiet. Keep me careful and keep me calm. Let tomorrow's weather be kind and my choices wise.
What do you do while you wait for the joy to come back?
The passage

paras.t: When Yahweh brought back those who returned to Zion, we were like those who dream. Then our mouth was filled with laughter, and our tongue with singing. Then they said among the nations, "Yahweh has done great things for them." Yahweh has done great things for us, and we are glad. Restore our fortunes again, Yahweh, like the streams in the Negev. Those who sow in tears will reap in joy. He who goes out weeping, carrying seed for sowing, will certainly come again with joy, carrying his sheaves.

Unless Yahweh builds the house, they labor in vain who build it. Unless Yahweh watches over the city, the watchman guards it in vain. It is vain for you to rise up early, to stay up late, eating the bread of toil; for he gives sleep to his loved ones.

spans.t: Reflection

Every long walk has a stretch that feels, afterwards, like a dream. A morning you cannot quite believe you walked. A day when the body did what you had been afraid it could not do. You tell it to yourself on the bench and it sounds a little made up.
Psalm 126 begins with that feeling, on a very large scale: the singers say
we were like those who dream

. The usual reading is that the singers are the people who came home from exile in Babylon, about the sixth century BC, though scholars differ on whether the song looks back at one event or many. Either way, it is the dazed joy of people who have got back what they thought was lost. Their mouths were full of laughter, and other nations noticed. Joy that large is visible from outside.
Then comes the turn that makes this a true song and not a greeting card. In the middle, the song turns from looking back to asking:
Restore our fortunes again, Yahweh, like the streams in the Negev.

They have come back, and they still ask for restoring. The Negev is the dry south of the land, where a riverbed can lie empty for months and then run with water after rain. The plea sits right beside the gladness, in the same song, with no embarrassment. Joy and unfinished business are neighbours. You reach the top of the pass and the other side is more road.
Then the best-known lines:
Those who sow in tears will reap in joy.

Commentators often point out that, in a poor year, sowing means putting into the ground the grain you might have eaten. The sower goes out because the field needs it, and weeps while he does it. The psalm does not tell him to stop weeping, or ask him to feel better first. He
goes out weeping, carrying seed

, the tears and the work carried together, one in each hand. For anyone who has set out on a walk because of a grief, this is the most honest sentence of the week so far. Nobody has to be finished with the crying before they walk.

That is the hard place, and it needs a plain word. It would be cruel to read the verse as a bargain: tears in, joy out. Some losses do not come round to joy, and some seasons are very long. What the psalm promises is that the sower will come back carrying sheaves, which is a promise about the harvest and not a promise that the harvest repays what was lost. If you are still in the weeping part, the song's concern is that you went out. That counts.
The second psalm of the day pushes the other way, against the opposite temptation.
Unless Yahweh builds the house, they labor in vain who build it.
Builders and watchmen are not told to stop. The psalm speaks to the one who has begun to think that it is all up to them:
It is vain for you to rise up early, to stay up late, eating the bread of toil; for he gives sleep to his loved ones.

Walkers know that temptation well. The earliest start. The longest day. The most kilometres, as though the road were an exam and the result were yours alone. The psalm does not say the work is pointless. It says the work is not all on you, and it ends not with effort but with sleep. You cannot earn sleep by staying up late, and you cannot hurry the morning by getting up in the dark.
So the two songs are a pair. One is for the person who weeps as they sow, the other for the one who worries as they build, and each ends in something received: sheaves, sleep.

There is one more hard place, in verses 3 to 5, which we left off the page. They praise children as a heritage and a quiver full of arrows, and a man glad of many sons to stand with him at the city gate. It was one world's idea of security, and it sits badly with those who have no children, or have lost one. If those verses have ever hurt you, you have company, and nothing else in the psalm depends on them.
Today's request is small. Carry the seed anyway, whatever it is, and let the tears come along if they want to. And give the day a proper end.
For the walk

items.t: Is there something I am pushing today that I could ease off for an hour, as though the day were not all up to me?

Choose one hour of today to walk without checking the pace, the distance or the time. When the hour is over, notice what you did not miss. If something heavy is walking with you, let it, and do not try to fix it. Carry it the way you would carry something that is for a purpose.

spans.t: At the end of the day

A day's work looks strange from a bed. You were so busy with it an hour ago, and now it is only a heap of small things that have stopped asking for anything. Let the heap sit there. You can look at it for a minute without sorting it.

What did you sow today? Not the great deeds, the small ones. A greeting that turned into a conversation. An hour spent beside someone slower than you. A word you decided not to say. Most of it you will never see grow, and that is the way of seed. You put it in the ground and you walk on.

Was there something today that felt like a dream? It may have been a view, or a moment of ease in the body, or a sudden lightness that had no reason. Name it. It does not need an explanation. And if there were tears, a few or many, the psalm does not make them a problem. They walk in the same company as the seed.

The second song speaks to anyone who is guarding something from a distance. You may have a house, a job, a person, a decision at home, and a quiet part of you has been standing watch over it all day, as the watchman stands on the wall. You cannot see it from here. Tonight the watch can be handed over. Say to yourself that it will keep until morning, and let the watchman off duty.
The psalm speaks of
the bread of toil

, and tonight's supper may be exactly that, eaten with sore legs. There is no scorn in the phrase. A day's effort is honest, and so is the meal after it. What the psalm refuses is only the idea that effort is the whole story.

Did anyone notice you today? In the first song, the other nations saw the joy and remarked on it. Perhaps a stranger smiled at you, or a host said you looked well. Joy shows more than we think, and it is allowed to.

The gift of the psalm is sleep, so make the end of the evening short. Wash, put your feet up for a few minutes, and let the body have the small things it has been waiting for all day. The mind builds a great many houses at two in the morning and they are almost always out of proportion. Do not plan tomorrow tonight beyond a start time and a bottle of water.

You may feel that today was not enough. Almost everyone does when tired. There are always more kilometres, more words, more care that you could have given. The psalm answers that gently: it is not all on you.

items.t: What did I put into the ground today, however small, that I will not see grow?
Where did something happen today that I could hardly believe?
What am I trying to carry alone that I could put down tonight and sleep on?

spans.t: A short prayer
Let the small things I planted today grow without me. Let the sorrow I carry walk beside me and not ahead of me. Take what I could not finish, and give me sleep. I will begin again when it is light.

chapters.title: Day 5. A table and a furrow

spans.t: What do you do with a blessing and a wound in the same day?
The passage

paras.t: Blessed is everyone who fears Yahweh, who walks in his ways. For you will eat the labor of your hands. You will be happy, and it will be well with you. Your wife will be as a fruitful vine, in the innermost parts of your house; your children like olive plants, around your table. Behold, thus is the man blessed who fears Yahweh. May Yahweh bless you out of Zion, and may you see the good of Jerusalem all the days of your life. Yes, may you see your children's children. Peace be upon Israel.

Many times they have afflicted me from my youth up. Let Israel now say, many times they have afflicted me from my youth up, yet they have not prevailed against me. The plowers plowed on my back. They made their furrows long. Yahweh is righteous. He has cut apart the cords of the wicked.

spans.t: Reflection
After a day on foot, bread is better than it has any right to be. A plain loaf, a bowl of soup, a few tomatoes: it tastes of the kilometres. Psalm 128 is a blessing about exactly that:
you will eat the labor of your hands.
The food is good because the day was work, and the work was yours.
The psalm opens on someone who
fears Yahweh
and
walks in his ways

, and both phrases need a little help. The fear is usually understood as reverence, a respectful awe, and not as fright. And walking is the oldest picture of how to live: a life is a walk. The blessing it offers is ordinary and rather lovely: work that feeds you, happiness, things going well, and a table.
And at the table, the household.
Your wife will be as a fruitful vine, in the innermost parts of your house; your children like olive plants, around your table.

Here we must be honest. The psalm speaks to a man, and the family is pictured from his chair. His wife is described and not addressed, and she is placed inside the house. The picture belongs to one kind of life in one kind of world. It leaves out a great many people: those who walk alone, whose table is small or empty, who have no children or have lost them, whose family is the reason they are on the road. The woman who is being described has her own day to get through, which the psalm does not mention.

Take what can be taken. A table with people round it as a picture of enough. Bread earned. New growth, olive shoots, around something steady. And remember that a walker is, by definition, away from the table. The blessing comes
out of Zion
, from the city, to someone at a distance, which is the position you are in. The road is not the opposite of home. It is a stretch of time away from the table, and the psalm blesses it.
Then Psalm 129 starts, and it is a different weather.
Many times they have afflicted me from my youth up.
It is a lifetime of harm, said twice, and said to the whole people:
Let Israel now say.
That is the same call as the song of the narrow escape, but this time it asks for a long memory and not a single rescue. The image is one of the hardest in the Psalms:
The plowers plowed on my back. They made their furrows long.
A back as a field. Anyone who carries an old wound, a body's or a heart's, knows what a furrow is. You carry a pack on that back too.
And yet:
yet they have not prevailed against me.
It is in the first sentence, as if the poet could not wait to say it. The harm was long, and it did not win. Then:
Yahweh is righteous. He has cut apart the cords of the wicked
, as though a harness had been cut from a plough team. The ploughed one is freed, and not by their own strength.

The harder part is in the verses we left out. In verses 5 to 8 the psalm turns from lament to curse. It asks that all who hate Zion be turned backward, that they be like grass on a rooftop, which withers before it grows, and that nobody passing should wish them a blessing. It reads as anger, said out loud by people who, as far as the song tells us, could do nothing but say it. Readers, Jewish and Christian, have handled such verses in different ways. Some read them as honest anger brought into prayer and not acted on. Some read them as a warning against becoming like the people who did the harm. Some set them aside. All of those are allowed here, and a book for walkers will not tell you to pray them.

One thing about the last verse, though, that belongs to the road. The curse ends with the wish that those who go by should not say a blessing. On a pilgrim road, blessing people who go by is the ordinary courtesy.
Buen Camino

, said in passing, is a small blessing of the very kind the psalm says is missing from the people it curses. You may say it to a stranger who irritates you. It costs nothing, and it is probably the best answer a walker has.

In an ordinary day that comes to three small things. Eat the bread slowly and be thankful for it. Carry old furrows without being defined by them. And bless somebody in passing, even if the blessing is only two words long.
For the walk

items.t: What old hurt am I carrying today, and can I name it to myself, without needing to do anything about it yet?
Say
Buen Camino

to every walker you pass today, including one you would rather not. Mean it as a small blessing and nothing more. You do not need to like them. If you are on a quiet stretch with no one in sight, say it to the next person you meet.

spans.t: At the end of the day

A table, if you have one tonight. If you do not, a bunk and a bag of bread will do, and so will a kitchen shared with strangers. Wherever you eat, eat slowly. It is the one meal of the day that is entirely deserved.

Who sat with you? Perhaps a few walkers whose names you will not keep. Perhaps no one, and you ate by the window with your phone. And who was missing? The people you left at home are at their own tables tonight, with your empty chair or without it. You may miss them most at supper. If your table at home is an easy one, that missing is a kind of wealth. If it is not, you may be glad of any table at all.
The psalm also says that the food is the labour of
your hands
, but tonight's bread was most likely other people's labour too: whoever grew it, baked it, cooked it, or carried it to the table. A thank-you can go to them as well.

Then the furrows. Long hours on foot give old hurts room to surface, in the dull miles when the mind has nothing to do. Perhaps one came up today. You are not asked to solve it tonight. Notice where it sits in the body: the shoulders, the jaw, the stomach. Naming a place is a start.

Notice, too, that in the song the hurt is said aloud, to the whole people, and not carried alone. Telling an old hurt to a listener is a different thing from carrying it in silence. If someone at your table tonight is a person you could trust with a little of it, you may find that a little is enough. If not, a page of a notebook can be a listener of sorts.

If you felt angry, at someone, at something that was done to you long ago, or only at the day, that is allowed too. The second psalm shows that anger can be put into words, even sharp ones, and that words are a better place for it than the next person you meet. Nothing needs doing with it before sleep.

Anger and tiredness are cousins, and they will lie down together if you let them. Do not decide anything big when you are both. The anger will still be there in the morning if it is real, and it will be easier to carry in daylight.

items.t: Who sat at my table today, in person or in thought, and who was missing?
What old hurt came up on the road, and where in my body did I feel it?
Whom could I bless tomorrow, even in one word, that I would normally walk past?

spans.t: A short prayer

For the bread I walked to, thank you. For the people at my table, near and far, keep them well. For the old hurt that came up today, let it lie down now. I am not asking to forget it, only to carry it lightly. Let me have one kind word ready for a stranger tomorrow.
What do you do when you cannot make the morning come?
The passage

paras.t: Out of the depths I have cried to you, Yahweh. Lord, hear my voice. Let your ears be attentive to the voice of my petitions. If you, Yah, kept a record of sins, Lord, who could stand? But there is forgiveness with you, therefore you are feared. I wait for Yahweh. My soul waits. I hope in his word. My soul longs for the Lord more than watchmen long for the morning; more than watchmen for the morning. Israel, hope in Yahweh, for with Yahweh there is loving kindness. With him is abundant redemption. He will redeem Israel from all their sins.

Yahweh, my heart isn't haughty, nor my eyes lofty; nor do I concern myself with great matters, or things too wonderful for me. Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with his mother, like a weaned child is my soul within me. Israel, hope in Yahweh, from this time forth and forevermore.

spans.t: Reflection

There is an hour, some time before dawn, when the dormitory is as quiet as it will get and you are awake. The pack is by the bed. Somebody is breathing slowly across the room. A thin line of light lies under the door. Everything you pushed aside during the walk now has room to sit up.
That is the hour of Psalm 130.
Out of the depths I have cried to you.
The picture is of a voice from a long way down, as from deep water. Notice how it begins. There is no request at first, only a plea to be heard:
Lord, hear my voice.
Before anything is asked for, the poet asks to be listened to. Anyone who has been awake in the dark knows how much that is.
Then a hard honest question.
If you, Yah, kept a record of sins, Lord, who could stand?
The picture is of a ledger kept on everyone, and the poet saying that nobody would come out well from it. The next line does not argue. It turns:
But there is forgiveness with you, therefore you are feared.
The oddity is the "therefore". The awe follows from the forgiveness and not in spite of it. The one before whom you could not stand is the one who lets you stand.
Then the waiting, in short plain pieces, like someone too tired for long sentences:
I wait for Yahweh. My soul waits. I hope in his word.
And the best image in the song:
My soul longs for the Lord more than watchmen long for the morning.

The watchmen are the sentries who keep a city's night watch. They are not hoping that morning will come, because they know it will. They are waiting for something certain, and the waiting is no shorter for that. The poet says it twice,
more than watchmen for the morning

, because that is what waiting sounds like. You say it again. For anyone awake at three, the lesson is a mild one. You cannot make the dawn come. You can only keep watch, and every morning of this walk has come so far.
Two places are hard. One is the word
sins

and the idea of a record. For some readers it is a tender and freeing word, and for others a heavy one, laden with guilt that was never theirs or shame they were handed. Read it, if you need to, as whatever you would rather were not on the record, and take the psalm's claim as it stands: that the record is not the last word.

The other is that the depths can be a good deal more than a bad night. Grief, fear, a darkness that does not lift by morning: the psalm gives such things a voice, and it does not say that the answer is quick. If what you carry is heavier than a walk can lighten, tell someone: a friend, a doctor, a helpline in your own country. If you are in danger of harming yourself, call 112 in Spain or France, or the emergency number where you are. Asking for help is no failure of the psalm. It is a good deal of what the psalm is about.
Psalm 131 is the quiet after.
Yahweh, my heart isn't haughty, nor my eyes lofty; nor do I concern myself with great matters, or things too wonderful for me.

The heading gives it to David, a king saying he has not set himself above anyone, which is an odd thing to say and a short song to say it in. What it describes is relief: no longer needing to master everything, to have a view on every question, or to settle your whole life on a road in Spain.
And then the picture of a quiet heart:
Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with his mother.
A weaned child is not a baby crying for milk. It is a child who has stopped demanding and rests against its mother's side, not for what it can get, only to be there. Notice the verbs:
I have stilled and quieted my soul.
The quiet is something made, with some effort, and not only given.

Some honest doubt belongs here. There will be days when the soul will not be stilled, and shouting at it makes it worse. The poet says the soul has been stilled. The psalm does not say how, or for how long, or what to do on the day it will not work. The nearest it comes to an answer is the child at the mother's side: be near what holds you, and stop asking for more.
For today, then, two things. Wait without pushing at the morning. And for one hour, set the great questions on a shelf, to be taken down later in daylight.
For the walk

items.t: What am I waiting for, and what would it be to wait for it for one hour without pushing at it?

For ten minutes today, walk without trying to work anything out. When a big question arrives, note it as you would a bird on a wire, and let it be. Then come back to the sound of your feet, your breath, the surface of the path.

spans.t: At the end of the day

The lights go out in the dormitory, or the house goes quiet, and the room begins its night noises. If you wake at three, you already know what to do. Do not fight it. Keep watch, as the sentries did. Watching is a task, not a failure, and morning is certain even if it is slow. If you like, find out now which way the window faces. Then, in the dark, you will know where the first light is going to come from.

Think back over the waiting that the day contained. There is always more than you notice: waiting for the village to appear round the next bend, for the blister to stop, for a café to open, for a message that has not come. What were you really waiting for under the smaller things? And where did you try to hurry it? A good deal of walking is pushing at mornings that arrive at their own pace.

Were there great matters in your head today? There usually are, a decision at home, a relationship, a question about the whole shape of your life. The road gives them room, and that is one of its gifts. It is also tiring to keep carrying them. The second psalm says that you are allowed to set them down for the night. They are not going anywhere. They will be there at breakfast, and a little easier to look at.

If the depths came up today, that was allowed. If they did not, be glad, and do not go looking for them. And if they are with you now, in the quiet, be honest about it with somebody, tomorrow if not tonight.

There may also be a small ledger of your own running tonight: the sharp word at four o'clock, the pace you pushed, the thing you forgot to do. The first psalm says that a record kept on everything is more than anyone could stand. You can close yours for the night. It is allowed to open again tomorrow, but not at three in the morning, when every entry is written in capitals.

The tired mind behaves very much like a tired child: it wants everything at once, it will not be reasoned with, and it cannot say what it needs. What the psalm describes, a child that has stopped demanding, is what a tired mind wants. The road to it often runs through food, warmth and lying down before it runs through thinking.

Tonight's practice is the child's. Lie down, let the bed take the weight of you, and for one minute stop holding up your own head. The mattress and the floor and the building have been holding up other people for years.

items.t: What am I waiting for, and where in the day did I try to hurry it?
Which great question could I set down tonight and leave until daylight?
Who is one person I could tell about whatever is heaviest, if I wanted to?

spans.t: A short prayer

Tonight I have no answers, and I will not ask for any. Keep watch with me until it is light. Let my mind be like a child that has stopped crying and is simply held. If I wake in the dark, let me wait without fear. The morning will come, and I will be here.

chapters.title: Day 7. Until I find a place

spans.t: What do you owe to the place where you lay your head, and to the people beside you?
The passage

paras.t: Yahweh, remember David and all his affliction, how he swore to Yahweh, and vowed to the Mighty One of Jacob: "Surely I will not come into the structure of my house, nor go up into my bed; I will not give sleep to my eyes, or slumber to my eyelids; until I find out a place for Yahweh, a dwelling for the Mighty One of Jacob." … "We will go into his dwelling place. We will worship at his footstool. Arise, Yahweh, into your resting place; you, and the ark of your strength. Let your priest be clothed with righteousness. Let your saints shout for joy!"

cite.t: — Psalm 132:1 to 5 and 7 to 9 (World English Bible)

paras.t: See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity! It is like the precious oil on the head, that ran down on the beard, even Aaron's beard; that came down on the edge of his robes; like the dew of Hermon, that comes down on the hills of Zion: for there Yahweh gives the blessing, even life forevermore.

spans.t: Reflection

Late in the afternoon, when the legs have gone and the day has been all slope, there is only one thought, and it is a bed. Not a view, not a story, not a better version of yourself: a place to put the pack down and lie flat. Every walker knows how much a single roof can weigh in the mind.
Psalm 132 begins with someone whose longing for a place was so great that he gave up his own.
Yahweh, remember David and all his affliction
, it says, and then it recalls an oath. The king would not go into his house or his bed.
I will not give sleep to my eyes
, he swore,
until I find out a place for Yahweh, a dwelling for the Mighty One of Jacob.
The place was for the ark, the chest at the heart of Israel's worship, which, according to the books of Samuel, David brought to Jerusalem.

Set that beside your own wish for a bed and it is a strange picture: a man who would not rest until someone else was housed. Psalm 127, on the fourth day, said that sleep is given to those who are loved, and today's psalm has a man who refused it. The two do not cancel. Some days you are the sleeper, and some days there is something you love that comes before sleep. But it is worth noticing how big a wish for a place can be, once it is pointed in the right direction.
Then the pilgrims, in their own voices.
We will go into his dwelling place.
The going in is plain and glad, and then comes a line a pilgrim might say at the end of a road:
Arise, Yahweh, into your resting place.
A resting place. The song is for people tired of travelling, who want the one they love to be somewhere restful too.

Most of what is hard is in the verses we left out, more than half the psalm. Verses 10 to 18 hold a promise to David's family, and the promise has a condition: if the king's children keep the covenant, their children will sit on the throne for ever. They also say that Zion is chosen as God's resting place, and they end with a line about enemies,
I will clothe his enemies with shame

. The psalm makes a claim about one city and one royal family, and many readers will find it hard to take as it stands. Christians have traditionally read the promise to David's line as pointing to Christ. Jewish readers have their own readings. We will not settle the matter here. Treat the line about enemies as you treated the harder verses of Psalm 129. What stays on the page is the longing for a place to rest.
Psalm 133 is three verses, and it might have been written about an albergue.
See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity!

Anyone who has shared a room with twenty strangers knows that unity is not automatic. The rustle of a plastic bag, a light that clicks on, the snore, the sock. The poem does not pretend it is easy. It says
see
, as though surprised, as though it had noticed something that does not usually happen. The word is
brothers
, and it was plainly meant of kin who belong in one household. On a road it stretches to everyone sharing the room.

The poem's two pictures are worth a minute each. Oil poured on the head of Aaron, the first high priest, running down the beard and onto the collar of his robes: abundant, a little extravagant, and not tidy. Then
the dew of Hermon
, from a high mountain a long way to the north of Jerusalem, falling on the hills of Zion: quiet, unseen, arriving in the night, so that you wake and everything is fresh.

Both are pictures of something coming down from above. Unity in this psalm is not built by effort. It descends, like oil or dew, and the invitation is to be in the place where it falls. At the end of a day on foot, that may be a table where strangers share what they have. Nobody has to agree about anything. They have one thing in common, which is that they walked here.
Unity is not the same as putting up with everything. If a room feels unsafe, that is a reason to speak to the host or to leave it, and the psalm has nothing against that.

So, at the end of an ordinary day, the psalms ask three things. Be glad of the roof and of whoever is under it. Make one small thing quieter. And let the common feeling of the room arrive, since it cannot be forced.
For the walk

items.t: Where do I want to rest at the end of this day, and what would it be to rest in the company as well as in the bed?
Before you arrive tonight, decide one small thing you will do for the room: fold your bag quietly, take your noise down, leave the kitchen cleaner than you found it. Do it without telling anyone.

spans.t: At the end of the day

A bed is a small, great thing. Whatever sort of place you found tonight, a bunk, a room, a corner on a floor, it is somewhere to put the day down. Before anything else, let yourself feel how good that is.

How did you find it? Perhaps it was easy. Perhaps it took a late walk, a knock, a worry, a "full" and a second try. Somebody made it possible. A person keeps the door, changes the sheets, switches the heating on. Whoever it was, they were doing it today, and most likely they will do it again tomorrow for someone else. If you can, thank them before you leave.

Then think about the people in the room. There were moments when they were a company and moments when they were only a crowd. There may have been a small shared laugh at supper that changed the temperature of the evening. Or no such moment at all, only a row of backs. Both happen. The psalm's dew arrives when it likes. You can only be outside when it falls. If you were the one who made the evening easier, even only by being quiet, that counts.

And the oil: was anything poured out generously today, more than you expected? An extra ladle, a shortcut offered, a long answer to a short question. Abundance on a road is usually small, and it goes where it is needed. Notice whether you were given some, and whether you passed some on.

Is there anything you would stay awake for, as David swore he would? A promise to someone at home, an apology that is overdue, a thing you meant to do before the walk started. You need not do it at midnight. But you might name it tonight, so that it does not go on being only a weight in the pocket. Writing it on a scrap of paper often moves it from the chest to the page.

If something about the room was hard, the noise, a stranger's habits, a bed too close, you do not need to turn it into a grievance tonight. Many of those things look different after sleep. If something was truly unsafe, tell someone tomorrow, or move now.

People are at their worst at living together when they are weary, and so the kindest thing you can do for a room is to be the first to be quiet. Put the phone down, wind the day up in a few minutes, and say good night aloud, in whatever language comes, to whoever is awake. It is the smallest dew there is, and it lands on everybody.

items.t: Where did I find a place to rest today, and who made it possible?
When did the people around me feel like a company, and when like a crowd?
What one small thing could I do tonight to make this room kinder to sleep in?

spans.t: A short prayer

Thank you for a roof, and for the people who keep it. Let this room be quiet and kind. Where there is friction, give us patience, and where there is none, let me notice it. Let me rest the way a good guest rests, grateful and easy. In the morning I will go out again.
What is said to you as you go?
The passage

paras.t: Look! Praise Yahweh, all you servants of Yahweh, who stand by night in Yahweh's house! Lift up your hands in the sanctuary. Praise Yahweh! May Yahweh bless you from Zion; even he who made heaven and earth.

spans.t: Reflection

Somewhere, tonight, someone is awake so that you can sleep. Perhaps it is the keeper of a hostel with a key in a pocket, or a nurse on a ward, or a driver on the ring road, or a baker whose day began at two. The world is full of people who work through the night, and most of us only meet them at the edge of the dark.
The last of the fifteen songs is for exactly those people. It calls to
all you servants of Yahweh, who stand by night in Yahweh's house.

These were, presumably, the ones who kept the watch in the house of worship while the city slept. Many scholars read the song as a call and an answer. The pilgrims, at the end of their visit, call out to the night staff, and a voice replies with a blessing. We cannot be sure it was first sung at a leaving, but it reads like one.
Look at how short it is, and at its verbs. The songs before it are full of going: going up, going out, coming in, turning back. This one is for those who
stand

. Yesterday, in Psalm 132, the pilgrims were on their way into the dwelling place. On the second day their feet were standing in the gate. Now the walking is over, and what is left is a place to stand and keep watch.
After eight days and fifteen songs of distress, of hills, of narrow places, of tears and furrows and depths, the book closes with three verses. There is not a request in them.
Lift up your hands in the sanctuary.

Hands lifted is a very old gesture. It can mean praise or asking, and it can simply mean that the hands are empty. A walker's hands are empty only at the end of the day, when the pack is down and the poles are in the corner. It is a good moment to lift them.
Praise Yahweh!
The collection that began with
In my distress, I cried to Yahweh

ends with praise. Notice that nothing has been solved. The lying lips of Psalm 120 are still out there. The furrows are still on the back from Psalm 129. The poet did not get an answer to every question, and the songs make no pretence that they did. Praise is not offered as a reward for fixing things. It is what comes next, after everything else has been said honestly. If the call to praise sounds too quick for you tonight, you do not have to force it. You can simply stay in the song.
Then the blessing, and a small change of voice. In the Hebrew, the first two verses are addressed to a crowd,
all you servants
, and the blessing turns to one person:
May Yahweh bless you from Zion; even he who made heaven and earth.
English cannot show it, since
you
does for one or for many. But the singular matters. After the long company of the road, the one who is leaving hears a word said over them alone.

A blessing is a word, and it cannot promise anything. A tired walker may feel foolish receiving one. It is not a guarantee, and the psalms in this book have been clear enough that nobody is guaranteed anything. What a blessing does is send someone after their journey with good will. It is like a cup handed through a window. You take it, and you drink, and you go on.

Now see what has come round. The line about the one who made heaven and earth is the third time we have met it in these eight days. It was the answer on the first day, to the question of the hills: help comes from the one
who made heaven and earth

. It came again at the end of the narrow escape. And now it ends the book. Whoever made the hills that frightened or called you on Day 1 is named, at the end, as the one who sends you off. And the blessing
from Zion
gathers up a line we met on the fifth day,
May Yahweh bless you out of Zion
, which was said over the table. The same hand blesses the table and the road.
There is a kind of circle in this. The first day gave us the going out and the coming in:
your going out and your coming in
. The last psalm is a going out again. The pilgrims set off from the house, with a blessing behind them.

Honest places? Not many here, but two. Much of this psalm is a call to people in a particular building doing a particular job, and most of us are not. We borrow it, as people have always borrowed the psalms. And the ending of a road is rarely tidy. You may feel relief and loss, or elation and flatness, in the same hour. The psalm makes no mention of either. It says only what is to be done with the hands and what is to be said.
What might it ask of an ordinary day? Thank somebody who keeps the night. Lift your empty hands once. And let yourself be blessed, then bless somebody else, since a blessing is meant to travel.
For the walk

items.t: Who keeps watch so that I can sleep, and have I ever thanked them?

At some point today, stop, put down whatever you are carrying, and lift your hands a little, palms open, for three breaths. Then wish something good, in your own words, on the next person you will meet. Walk on. If you cannot manage it aloud, do it in your head; the hands are the part that matters.

spans.t: At the end of the day

This may be the last evening of the book, and perhaps of the walk. Last evenings are strangely tiring. The body has been told that it can stop, and it takes that rather literally. If you feel elated and flat at once, that is understandable, and it is not a sign that something has gone wrong.

Look back over today, and over the days before it, as you would look at a road from the top of a pass. It began with a cry and a question about hills. There was gladness at a gate, a narrow place, some tears and a long day of work, an old furrow, a night with no sleep, a roof and a room full of strangers. None of it has to become a lesson. It happened, and you were there.

Give the ending a minute before you do anything with it. The mind wants to run ahead to the journey home, the photographs, the things you will tell people, the next walk. All of that can wait. A last evening is a good one to do nothing with, to sit with your hands empty and let what happened settle where it will.
Look at your hands for a moment. They held the poles, tore the bread, gripped the rail on the steps. Lift them a little, open, as the psalm says, and then lay them down on the blanket.

Who kept watch for you today? Not in a grand way. The person who put the light on at the corner, the one who left the door unlatched, the family at home who kept the evening free for your call. Many of the people who hold us up do it by night or at a distance, and we only notice when we are tired enough to be grateful. If there is someone to thank, you could do it now, in a line, or write it on a card for the morning.

Then, if you will let it, receive the blessing. It is a plain thing: a wish for your good, said in the singular, with all the weight of those who have said it before. A wish can be received without believing anything. You only have to be willing to be wished well.
And if the walk goes on tomorrow, take the blessing with you. The psalm sends the pilgrim out the way a host sends a guest to the door.
And sleep. Someone is awake, and you do not have to be.

items.t: Who kept watch for me today, in ways I only half noticed?
Over whom would I like to say a blessing before I sleep: a person, a place, the road itself?
What am I taking home from these days that I did not bring?

spans.t: A short prayer

Thank you for everyone who keeps the night so that others can sleep. Thank you for the road, the hills and the roof. Bless the people I will meet and the ones I have left. Bless me too, and send me on. I will sleep now.

The eight days are over, or you have stopped early, or you mean to start again from the top. Any of these will do. Nobody is keeping a record. The book was only ever meant to walk beside you for a while, and it does not mind whether your road ended at Puente la Reina, somewhere short of it, or at your own front door.
That leaves one question: what to keep. Not the whole book, since nobody carries that. Three suggestions, and you may ignore all of them.

items.t: Learn one by heart.

Psalms 131, 133 and 134 are only three verses long, and Psalm 121 is eight. A psalm learned on foot makes a good companion, because the walking keeps time for it and because it is the right length for a mile or two. Say it under your breath on a bad hill, or in the queue for the kitchen.
Keep one small habit.
Lifting the eyes at a rise. A wish of peace on a village. A thank-you aloud after a narrow place.
Buen Camino
to someone you would rather not greet. Open hands for three breaths. Pick the one that cost you least and helped most, and do it again tomorrow.
Read what was left out.

Six of the fifteen psalms were quoted in part. In any Bible you can find the rest: verses 3 and 4 of Psalm 120, verse 5 of Psalm 122, verses 3 to 5 of Psalms 125 and 127, verses 5 to 8 of Psalm 129, and most of Psalm 132. Read them slowly and aloud, and notice which you can say and which you cannot. Remember that some Bibles number the psalms one lower.

spans.t: How to go on

You can go back to any day. They are short on purpose, and some will say more to you a month from now than they did on the morning you read them. Try them in a different order. Try the evenings only. Or keep one passage for a bad morning and say it aloud.

Be honest, too, about what did not work. Some of these psalms ask for things you may not be able to give: harm wished on enemies, a household drawn too narrowly, a promise that the sun will never hurt you. That is allowed, and it is no failing in you. A day that did not speak to you has done no harm. Leave it where it is.
A last word

If the tradition is right, the people who first sang these songs did not stay in the city. They went up, and they went home. The last song reads like a sending-off, and the blessing in it is meant to go with the one who leaves. Going home is the second half of a pilgrimage, and often the harder half.
The first day gave you a line about
your going out and your coming in

. It is a good one to end on, because it describes a life as well as a walk. You go out, and you come in, and then, if the weather holds, you go out again. Nothing in it asks you to be certain, or finished. It asks for a next step, some patience with yourself, and, when one comes, a kindness from a stranger that you can pass on.
Buen Camino.
